results.note: Confirmed in Comment paragraph 13: it begins at the bottom of the right column of printed p. 2078 (PDF4) and continues at the top of the left column of p. 2079 (PDF5). The author states eight eyewitnessed deaths with a dash of a few hundred feet followed by collapse, then explicitly leaves the terminal event uncertain among the listed possibilities and unknown factors. This is an observation of a sequence and an uncertain mechanistic interpretation, not recorded arrhythmia or evidence that exertion caused death. The paragraph itself refers to cases 1-5; the eight must not be added to the six narrated eyewitness accounts or the 18 activity/stress entries as nonoverlapping deaths. The surrounding statement appropriately preserves the author's uncertainty. No correction needed.

Confirmed at Background paragraph 3 on p. 2075 (PDF1) and Comment paragraphs 2, 3 and 7 on p. 2078 (PDF4). Paragraph 2 names the three fluorocarbons; paragraph 3 reports very low acute-inhalation toxicity in rats and guinea pigs; paragraph 7 attributes the least-toxic-chlorinated-aliphatic-solvent assessment to Stewart and Andrews' reported human toxicological data. The Background separately says some involved products were considered low toxicity on human and animal experimental evidence. These are historical assessments and cited experimental evidence recounted by Bass, not measurements from the 110-death survey or evidence that the products were safe for intentional inhalation. The qualifier maintains that scope. No correction needed.

Confirmed in Results 3.4 paragraph 4 on p. 172 (PDF5) and Table 6 on p. 173 (PDF6), including its n=55 footnote and permission for more than one reason. The four printed motive percentages are 45.5, 32.7, 21.8 and 18.2; compatible counts given 55 are respectively 25, 18, 12 and 10. The product-source percentages 34, 32.1, 30.2 and 28.3 appear in the same Results paragraph; the article also lists friend at 7.5%, which this nonexhaustive extraction omits. A denominator for the product-source shares is not specified there and should not be assumed to be the 55 reason respondents. These motives are self-reported aims, not demonstrated effects, and the pleasure motive is pooled across preloading/postloading rather than linked to a particular product. No correction needed.

All four association summaries, group percentages, age means and printed statistics match Results 3.4's final paragraph on p. 173 (PDF6). Methods 2.4 p. 170 (PDF3) lists 10 variables and specifies analyses for changing use in response to dislikes, preloading and postloading: 10 x 3 = at least 30 focal comparisons, an editorial reconstruction rather than an author-reported test count. Results 3.2 pp. 170-171 explicitly adds three sex comparisons and three correlations; the full additional test count is unrecoverable because only significant gender differences are reported. No multiplicity adjustment is described; the stated alpha 0.025 for violated normality is a separate rule. Compatible two-by-two reconstructions reproduce chi-square 7.16, 6.58 and 4.38 and the printed p-value rounding. The age t statistic cannot be reconstructed from the two means alone. 'No other respondent variable' is supported as a summary of the reported analyses of these outcomes, not a universal null statement. These are bivariate, cross-sectional associations and retain differing denominators (116, 114 and age df 113). No correction needed.

Confirmed in the cited source spans. The comedown definition occurs in the p. 169 (PDF2) Introduction paragraph beginning 'Ecstasy users are known'; 'second paragraph' is readable as the second paragraph appearing on that page, including the preceding continued paragraph, rather than the second paragraph of the whole Introduction. Method 2.1 explicitly excludes efficacy from the study focus; Method 2.3 pp. 169-170 describes the prompted strategy list and separately asks pill-testing and preloading/postloading frequencies. It gives no validation/piloting account or reference period for the prompted list, and Discussion paragraph 4 p. 173 explicitly says frequency of those strategies was not asked. Discussion paragraph 2 p. 173 gives the possible online-recruit interest caveat. Paragraphs 11-14 pp. 174-175 recount the animal evidence, injection/rodent limits and serotonin-syndrome caution, with no interaction outcomes in this sample. The p. 175 limitations paragraph identifies retrospective self-report, cross-sectional associations and unknown recruitment-method return breakdown. Absence of validation reporting is not proof that validation never occurred. Rodent evidence and interaction cautions are the authors' narrative claims, not findings newly tested here or independently checked against cited primary studies. The qualification is appropriately scoped. No correction needed.

Independently reconstructed from N=116 in Results 3.1 p. 170, 41.4%/47.4% in Results 3.4 p. 172, Table 5's 41.3% and n=46 on p. 172, and Table 6's 45.5% and n=55 on p. 173. At the assumed/stated denominators, the compatible counts are uniquely 48, 55, 19 and 25 under ordinary rounding to one decimal; this does not establish possession of the raw data or resolve unstated item nonresponse. Wilson score 95% without continuity correction gives 32.8335-50.4778%, 38.5564-56.4370%, 28.2886-55.6605% and 33.0253-58.4773%, reproducing all four proposed one-decimal intervals. Half-widths are 8.8222, 8.9403, 13.6859 and 12.7260 percentage points, supporting about 9 versus about 12-14. The article does not present these confidence intervals or the reconstructed numerators. Table 5 has n=46 preloading and n=54 postloading product lists; Table 6 has n=55 pooled reasons, distinct from the whole-sample ever-use denominators. Multiple responses were allowed. These intervals describe arithmetic sampling precision under binomial assumptions and do not correct self-selection, dependence, missingness or broader measurement limitations. No correction needed.
